results.summary: This design implements several free-running oscillators built from combinational loops with dividers to bring the output frequency below 50 kHz. Input pins select which oscillator source is active, and output pins expose the generated clock along with divided versions at several powers of two. A true random number generator output is also provided on one pin, and a shift register interface allows configuration. The project is intended to compare simulation against silicon reality and requires an external frequency measurement instrument such as an oscilloscope or counter.

This Verilog design generates a PWM signal whose duty cycle is selected by three digital input signals, with an enable input gating operation. The duty cycle steps in 12.5% increments from 12.5% to 100% depending on the three-bit input combination. Testing requires a 10 MHz clock source and an oscilloscope to observe the pulse width at the output. The documentation is in Spanish and describes a straightforward educational PWM generator.

This Wokwi project uses OR gate logic to drive a seven-segment LED display so that it shows the letter J. Eight input pins are connected to switches, and eight output pins drive the display segments. The user flips switches to produce the letter J on the display. The documentation is minimal and the external hardware section is left as a template placeholder, so the exact wiring is not fully specified.

This design implements Wolfram's Rule 30 one-dimensional cellular automaton in hardware and renders it on a VGA monitor. A 320-bit register holds each generation, updating all cells in parallel every row, with 480 rows showing 480 generations of evolution from a central seed. Two input pins select among four color palettes, and the VGA output uses the Tiny VGA pinout. It requires a VGA monitor and Pmod connected to the output pins, and the result is the characteristic chaotic triangular pattern.

This is an analog double-inverter buffer consisting of two inverters, one large and one small, connected in series. The analog input is on one pin and the buffered analog output is on another. It originates from Matt's analog course and is intended as a test structure to verify analog simulation against silicon. No external hardware is required beyond the analog signal source and measurement equipment.

This Wokwi project is a puzzle game where flipping any of seven switches toggles a corresponding segment on a seven-segment display along with its neighboring segments. The goal is to reach configurations that display all numbers from 0 to 9. Seven input pins connect to microswitches and seven output pins drive the display segments, excluding the decimal point. It requires an external seven-segment LED display and seven microswitches to play.

This Verilog design generates a controllable Archimedean spiral pattern (r = theta) rendered on a VGA display. Eight input pins allow changing the foreground and background colors and the speed of the spiral animation. It requires a VGA Pmod connected to the output pins and a 25 MHz clock, with optional switches for control. The documentation is brief but describes the core function and testing setup.

This Verilog design classifies images of digits from 0 to 7 using 16 selected pixels from an 8x8 image as input features. The classification result is shown on a seven-segment display via eight output pins. Input features are provided on the ui and uio pins, and the documentation gives an example of setting features for the digit zero. No external hardware is required, and the project appears to be an educational exercise in simple image classification.

This design is a time-multiplexed spiking neural network accelerator implementing four leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with a 4x4 synapse matrix. Weights are held off-chip by an RP2040 and streamed in via PIO, keeping the transistor count under 2000. The FSM processes one neuron at a time in seven states, achieving about 1.78 million network passes per second at 50 MHz, and supports Hebbian learning pulses. Testing requires an RP2040 running the provided PIO firmware, though a minimal smoke test can be done without it by injecting spikes and observing outputs.

This Verilog project is a loopback tile that counts up to 10, one second at a time, and includes input skew measurement. It uses input pins for compare bits, bidirectional pins for a second counter, and output pins for a seven-segment display. The documentation is essentially unwritten, with 'Need to write this' for both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections. External hardware includes programmable delay lines on the inputs, but the design's exact operation cannot be determined from the available text.
